Chapter 6. Good, Evil, and the Dance of Contraries.
As we move deeper into the collection, Blake starts to ask a question that’s just as relevant today as it was in his time—what does it really mean to be good? And, just as important, what is evil?
The poems don’t hand us simple answers. Instead, they invite us into a world where life is made up of opposites—joy and sorrow, innocence and experience, light and shadow. And it’s right in the middle of that push and pull, in the tension between those opposites, that we start to find meaning.
Picture two friends, sitting across from each other, maybe with coffee or tea, debating late into the night. One says, “We need rules. Order keeps us safe.” The other shakes their head, “But too many rules? They just crush your spirit.” The talk gets intense, but underneath it all, both of them just want to understand.
That’s where Blake’s poems come alive—in the space where opposites meet and spark something new.
There’s a poem about someone who feels caught between kindness and anger. They want to forgive, but old hurts still sting. The poem doesn’t judge or take sides—it just sits with that struggle.
Pretty soon, you realize good and evil aren’t these fixed labels. They’re more like forces that move through every life, every choice. Most of us feel like we have to pick a side, but the poems hint that wisdom comes from learning to hold both at once.
Blake’s verses are full of fire and tenderness. In one poem, a figure rages against injustice, their words sharp and powerful. In another, someone kneels quietly, whispering a prayer for mercy.
The poems never say which one is right. Instead, Blake shows how both are needed—how anger can shake things up and push for change, while forgiveness can bring real healing.
There’s another layer, too—evil isn’t always easy to spot. Sometimes, it hides behind good manners or old traditions. In one poem, someone does what’s expected, even though it feels wrong deep down. You can almost feel the quiet ache of betraying yourself just to fit in.
The poems nudge us to look closer, to question what we’ve always been told.
But it’s not all struggle. Blake also lifts up the everyday moments of courage. A child stands up to a bully. A worker speaks out when something’s unfair. These might seem small, but the poems remind us—those choices matter.
Goodness, it seems, shows up in those little acts, day after day.
By the end of this section, you can see how the poems have woven together a tapestry of opposites. They don’t hand you easy answers, but they do offer something else—a way of living that embraces all the messiness, that finds beauty right in the heart of life’s dance of contraries.
